author: sonnet
reason: B is quicker to follow: its summary splits the run into three steps (extract, stage, commit), it lists what starts each step, and it shows the commit transaction as actual SQL; A covers rationale and edge cases in more depth but takes longer to read.

author: sonnet
reason: B gives an outsider more context: it says why the design looks the way it does (no write access to the app database, the fixed 06:00 dashboard refresh), defines every component including the scheduler and the per-attempt cutoff, walks the attempt step by step, and states its timeout, timing budget, clock assumptions and open questions, where A is tighter but takes more for granted.

author: haiku
reason: A opens with a plain-language walkthrough, defines every term it relies on, and explains why each mechanism exists (claims that store a stamp reference, closing a day by log offsets, the ledger), and its failure table shows what each fault does and what someone would see; B is easier to scan thanks to its diagram, but it leaves key mechanics such as day closing and the replay grace period less settled and less explained.

author: haiku
reason: B is the one I would rather be handed: it opens with a plain-prose walk through the live and replay paths, says why the system is built this way (clients retry, so every copy is kept and one rule picks the winner), and adds a failure table showing what happens and what an operator sees, so a newcomer learns both the mechanism and the reasoning, though its day-close section is denser than A's short diagram and glossary.

author: sonnet
reason: B is quicker to get oriented in: a data-flow diagram up front, a "decisions that shape everything" section that gives the reasons, and steps grouped by component. A explains the same ideas with equal rigor, and its failure table is useful, but its numbered prose takes more effort to turn into a picture of the system.

author: sonnet
reason: A opens with a data-flow diagram of the live and replay paths and a "decisions that shape everything" section, then walks the components in the order data moves through them, so a newcomer gets the whole mental model before the details. B has a good prose overview and a failure table, but it puts assumptions and the open bot-traffic question ahead of the system description and has no diagram.

author: haiku
reason: A explains the runtime flow from end to end (click, job, page, failures) with every term defined up front and a failure table that sums up each failure, and it keeps build and rollout steps apart from how the system runs; B puts build steps such as the shared module and the migration into its runtime sequence and leaves more concurrency details vague.

author: haiku
reason: B begins with the context an outsider lacks (what the page does, why the work splits at 10,000 rows, what is out of scope), keeps how the feature runs apart from how it gets built, and its failure table shows the whole system on one screen, while also pointing out behaviour A leaves implicit, such as the unfiltered row count and the per-attempt file keys.

author: sonnet
reason: A starts by describing the existing system (the rows API, the replica, the view stored in the URL) and defines the existing infrastructure up front (jobs.py retry and timeout behaviour, storage.py multipart rules, bucket lifecycle). It then walks one linear flow with a failure table, so a newcomer can follow it on their own; B leaves those facts scattered across its steps, adds an optional extra step, and points to requirements and a conversation the reader never saw.

author: sonnet
reason: B is easier for a newcomer to follow, because it describes what already exists before the new design: the rows API, the URL-held view, jobs.py and storage.py. It also says why the large path is needed (the 60 s request kill and the roughly 900 MB report), and it adds a failure table and a test list that make the flow concrete, while A starts straight into the design and treats the queue and storage as already known.

author: haiku
reason: A covers every path from start to finish and stays consistent with itself: the cache miss, a Key Service outage, Enterprise and missing plans skipping the check, the window computed on Redis's clock, plus a failure table and launch checks. B leaves the Key Service outage out of scope, draws Enterprise going through a check that has no limit, mixes the gateway and Redis clocks, and cites "requirement N" items that a newcomer cannot see.

author: haiku
reason: B is the better handover: it opens with a plain summary of the current flow and why the design is shaped this way, then walks through every step, failures included. It covers the cache miss and the Key Service outage, and its failure table shows for each case what the client gets, whether the request is forwarded and whether the counter changes. Its script uses Redis's clock for both the window key and Retry-After, while A mixes the gateway's clock with Redis's and leaves the Enterprise and Key Service paths unclear.

author: sonnet
reason: A starts by explaining how the gateway works today (stateless instances, the Key Service, the per-instance 5-minute cache) before it adds the change, ties its notes to numbered diagram steps, and covers more edge cases (a plan change mid-window, a timeout after the script already ran, a failure table), so an outsider gets a more complete and grounded picture than from B's shorter but thinner account.

author: sonnet
reason: B is the one I would rather be handed: it first explains how the gateway works today, then adds terms, a failure table, rollout steps and clearly marked unknowns, such as plan changes mid-window and the timeout firing after Redis already ran the script; its step-number references to the autonumbered diagram are off, but its fuller context still beats A's tighter, more self-contained walkthrough.
